guides.title: Behavioral
guides.intro: Prepare to explain real experiences and introduce yourself clearly. Questions about past behavior ask what you actually did; broader questions explore your interests and direction.

blocks.title: Choose a real example
blocks.text: Use work, coursework, projects or volunteering that you can discuss honestly. Briefly establish the context, then focus on your own decisions. An imperfect outcome can still show learning.

blocks.title: Use STAR for a past experience
blocks.text: Situation: set the scene. Task: explain your responsibility. Action: describe your contribution and reasoning. Result: explain the outcome, evidence and learning. The practice workspace has optional STAR fields.

blocks.title: Use a different structure for introductions
blocks.text: For an introduction, connect your current focus, one relevant experience and what you want to do next. For motivation or strengths, state your point, support it and connect it to the role. You do not need to force every answer into STAR.

questions.title: Introduce yourself
questions.prompt: Give a brief introduction connecting your current focus, a relevant experience and the kind of contribution you want to make next.
structure: Current focus: what are you working on or learning?
Relevant experience: what demonstrates that interest?
Next step: why does this opportunity fit?
look_for: A clear thread between experience and direction.
One concrete detail, with room for follow-up.
mistakes: Reciting your entire resume.
Inventing a polished achievement to fill a gap.

questions.title: Explain your interest
questions.prompt: What interests you about this role or field, and which part of your experience helped you decide?
structure: Name a specific aspect of the work.
Connect it to a real experience or interest.
Explain what you want to contribute or learn.
look_for: A reason tied to actual tasks.
An honest distinction between experience and aspiration.
mistakes: Only praising the company.
Claiming to know an employer you have not researched.

questions.title: Support a strength
questions.prompt: Choose a strength relevant to your target work. What is a specific example of you using it, and where are its limits?
structure: Name a relevant strength.
Give a brief supporting example.
Explain its application and limitations.
look_for: Observable actions rather than personality labels.
mistakes: Listing unsupported adjectives.
Presenting a preference as proof of ability.

questions.title: Discuss an area to develop
questions.prompt: Describe something you are actively improving, the steps you are taking and how you will know you are making progress.
structure: Identify a specific development target.
Explain your practice or feedback process.
Describe progress and a next check.
look_for: Evidence appropriate to your current stage.
mistakes: Disguising a strength as a weakness.
Claiming the issue is solved without evidence.

questions.title: Work with a team
questions.prompt: Describe a time your team needed to coordinate different contributions. How did you help the work come together?
structure: Set the situation and responsibility briefly.
Describe your own actions and why you chose them.
Explain the result you can support and what you learned.
look_for: How you handled dependencies or misunderstandings.
mistakes: Saying only what we did.
Taking credit for the whole team.

questions.title: Handle a disagreement
questions.prompt: Think of a disagreement about how to do a task. What did you do to understand the other view and move the work forward?
structure: Set the situation and responsibility briefly.
Describe your own actions and why you chose them.
Explain the result you can support and what you learned.
look_for: How you listened and explained your reasoning.
mistakes: Blaming the other person.
Inventing an effortless resolution.

questions.title: Take initiative
questions.prompt: Describe a time you noticed a problem or opportunity and took a useful first step without being asked.
structure: Set the situation and responsibility briefly.
Describe your own actions and why you chose them.
Explain the result you can support and what you learned.
look_for: Why the step was useful and appropriate.
Who you involved and what you checked.
mistakes: Equating initiative with ignoring constraints.
Claiming an impact you did not measure.

questions.title: Learn from a setback
questions.prompt: Choose a task that did not go as you expected. How did you respond, and what would you change next time?
structure: Set the situation and responsibility briefly.
Describe your own actions and why you chose them.
Explain the result you can support and what you learned.
look_for: A specific lesson applied or planned.
mistakes: Hiding your part in the problem.
Replacing the outcome with a made-up success.

questions.title: Manage competing priorities
questions.prompt: Describe a time two responsibilities competed for your time. How did you decide what to do and communicate the tradeoff?
structure: Set the situation and responsibility briefly.
Describe your own actions and why you chose them.
Explain the result you can support and what you learned.
mistakes: Claiming you completed everything perfectly.
Skipping the actual tradeoff.

questions.title: Use feedback
questions.prompt: Describe feedback that led you to change your approach. What did you change and how did you check whether it helped?
structure: Set the situation and responsibility briefly.
Describe your own actions and why you chose them.
Explain the result you can support and what you learned.
mistakes: Treating feedback as a personal attack.
Reporting agreement without a change in behavior.

guides.title: Case / business
guides.intro: Work through an unfamiliar business problem aloud. These are original fictional exercises; the goal is to explain a useful line of reasoning, not memorize a firm’s case answers.

blocks.title: Frame the decision
blocks.text: Clarify the objective, the decision-maker and the constraints before calculating. State what you know, what you assume and what you would ask next.

blocks.title: Make the reasoning visible
blocks.text: Break the problem into a few relevant parts, use units consistently and explain what each finding changes. Revise your approach when new information arrives.

blocks.title: Finish with a recommendation
blocks.text: Give a decision, its strongest reasons, risks and a next test. Acknowledge information that could change your answer.

questions.title: Investigate falling profit
questions.prompt: A fictional campus cafe reports steady weekly sales but a 20% fall in profit. What would you clarify and investigate before recommending action?
structure: Clarify how profit and sales are measured.
Separate price, volume and cost drivers.
Prioritize evidence and a reversible next step.
look_for: A testable explanation rather than a guess.
mistakes: Assuming revenue equals profit.
Cutting staff before understanding the cause.

questions.title: Estimate demand
questions.prompt: A fictional bicycle repair service is considering weekend appointments in a university district. How would you estimate demand and test whether the service is worth offering?
structure: Define the area, time period and potential customers.
Build an estimate with explicit assumptions and units.
Check sensitivity and propose a small pilot.
look_for: A useful way to validate uncertain inputs.
mistakes: Inventing population statistics as facts.
Presenting a single estimate with no uncertainty.

questions.title: Reduce waiting time
questions.prompt: A fictional community workshop has a growing appointment queue. Adding staff is one option, but the bottleneck is unknown. How would you diagnose it?
structure: Map the steps and arrival patterns.
Identify where work waits and what to measure.
Compare changes and monitor outcomes.
look_for: A measure that reflects the customer experience.
mistakes: Optimizing a step that is not the bottleneck.
Assuming averages describe every busy period.

questions.title: Assess a new offering
questions.prompt: A fictional stationery business can launch either a low-cost refill pack or a premium gift set with the same small budget. How would you compare the options?
structure: Clarify the goal and target customer.
Compare demand, contribution and operational risk.
Recommend a test with decision criteria.
look_for: What evidence would reverse the recommendation.
mistakes: Choosing solely from personal taste.
Ignoring the cost of acquiring customers.

questions.title: Design a useful experiment
questions.prompt: A fictional online course sees many registrations but few completions. The team proposes reminder messages. How would you test the idea?
structure: Define completion and the population.
Compare an appropriate test group and baseline.
Choose outcome, guardrail and follow-up measures.
look_for: How results would inform a decision.
mistakes: Assuming every dropout needs a reminder.
Calling an observed difference causal without a design.

questions.title: Make a constrained recommendation
questions.prompt: A fictional nonprofit must choose between extending opening hours and improving remote access. Funds support only one pilot. How would you make and explain the choice?
structure: Identify users, needs and constraints.
Compare benefits, costs and accessibility.
Recommend a pilot, risks and a review point.
mistakes: Treating all users as identical.
Ignoring people excluded by the preferred option.

guides.title: Domain / scenario
guides.intro: Practice explaining professional reasoning in a field. Each example below is fictional and can be adapted to your level; it does not establish credentials or permission to perform regulated work.

blocks.title: Set the boundaries
blocks.text: Name the role you are answering from, the objective and the missing facts. Distinguish a hypothetical response from work you have actually done.

blocks.title: Reason, check and communicate
blocks.text: Explain a first step, alternatives, checks and what you would communicate. State what needs supervision, verification or escalation rather than bluffing.

blocks.title: Choose a relevant field
blocks.text: Use the field on each card to choose an example. For personalized practice, add your role and focus in setup, or supply a question from your own preparation materials.

questions.title: Investigate inconsistent data
questions.prompt: Fictional scenario: two dashboards disagree about the same weekly total. As a junior analyst, explain how you would investigate and communicate the discrepancy.
structure: Confirm definitions, time windows and source versions.
Trace a small sample through the transformations.
Report findings, uncertainty and the next check.
look_for: When you would ask a data owner for help.
mistakes: Choosing the larger total without investigation.
Changing production data before checking authority.

questions.title: Check a supplier recommendation
questions.prompt: Fictional scenario: a team wants to change suppliers based on a cheaper quote that excludes delivery costs. How would you support a sound comparison?
structure: Clarify requirements and compare like-for-like costs.
Identify quality, timing and contract questions.
Communicate the tradeoff and seek missing evidence.
mistakes: Treating the quoted price as total cost.
Making commitments outside your authority.

questions.title: Respond to an unexpected test result
questions.prompt: Fictional scenario: a prototype test returns a result outside the expected range shortly before a review. As an engineering team member, what would you check and communicate?
structure: Record the anomaly and test conditions.
Check assumptions and measurement reliability within your role.
Raise safety or competence concerns with the responsible lead.
look_for: A clear separation between investigation and approval.
mistakes: Discarding an inconvenient result.
Claiming design approval or expertise you do not hold.

questions.title: Handle a privacy concern
questions.prompt: Fictional scenario: while helping with appointment administration, you notice a patient list on a shared screen visible to visitors. What would you do within an administrative role?
structure: Describe the immediate privacy concern without repeating personal data.
Follow the organization’s process and notify an appropriate supervisor.
Explain what you would document and verify.
look_for: Recognition that clinical decisions require qualified staff.
mistakes: Sharing patient details in the interview.
Offering medical advice or inventing local policy.

questions.title: Adapt an explanation
questions.prompt: Fictional scenario: in a supervised learning activity, several learners misunderstand the same instruction. How would you adjust the explanation and check understanding?
structure: Clarify the learning goal and observed misunderstanding.
Offer an accessible alternative within your role.
Check understanding and seek guidance if needed.
look_for: Evidence of learning rather than assumptions.
mistakes: Labelling learners from one interaction.
Assuming repetition alone proves understanding.

questions.title: Resolve an unclear creative brief
questions.prompt: Fictional scenario: a client asks for a design that is both minimal and packed with detail. How would you clarify the brief and move toward a reviewable proposal?
structure: Ask about audience, purpose and constraints.
Show a small set of alternatives and explain tradeoffs.
Agree on feedback and revision criteria.
look_for: A clear interpretation of the brief.
Your contribution and permission to share work.
mistakes: Dismissing the client’s concern.
Presenting another person’s work as your own.

questions.title: Examine a result that will not reproduce
questions.prompt: Fictional scenario: a public-data analysis gives a different result when a colleague reruns it. How would you investigate before drawing a conclusion?
structure: Compare data versions, methods and environments.
Reproduce a small example and record deviations.
Communicate limits and agree on further checks.
mistakes: Changing the method just to recover a desired result.
Claiming an unverified scientific finding.

guides.title: Presentation / portfolio
guides.intro: Explain a real artifact, project or presentation so someone can understand the purpose, your contribution and the evidence behind your choices.

blocks.title: Select rather than catalogue
blocks.text: Choose work you are allowed to share that fits the audience and role. Explain the brief, show a useful detail and identify your individual contribution.

blocks.title: Build a clear story
blocks.text: Use a purpose → decisions → evidence → reflection structure. For a short presentation, lead with the key point and use supporting material selectively.

blocks.title: Prepare for discussion
blocks.text: Anticipate questions about alternatives, limitations and revisions. Separate completed work from proposed next steps and acknowledge collaborators.

questions.title: Explain the purpose
questions.prompt: Choose a real artifact you can share. What problem or need did it address, and who was it for?
structure: State the need and audience.
Show the relevant part of the artifact.
Explain what success meant.
look_for: A specific purpose and selection rationale.
mistakes: Starting with every implementation detail.

questions.title: Make your contribution clear
questions.prompt: Walk through a collaborative project and explain which decisions and deliverables were yours.
structure: Set the project context.
Distinguish your work from collaborators’ work.
Show evidence of one contribution.
mistakes: Claiming the entire project as individual work.

questions.title: Defend a decision
questions.prompt: Pick one important decision in your work. Which alternatives did you consider, and why did you choose this approach?
structure: Describe the constraint or decision.
Compare plausible alternatives.
Explain your choice and its limitations.
mistakes: Claiming the chosen approach had no tradeoffs.

questions.title: Explain what you checked
questions.prompt: How did you evaluate whether an artifact, analysis or presentation achieved its purpose?
structure: Define the intended outcome.
Explain the checks or feedback you used.
Distinguish findings from remaining uncertainty.
look_for: Checks that relate to the stated purpose.
mistakes: Treating a polished appearance as proof of success.

questions.title: Adapt to an audience
questions.prompt: Give a short explanation of your work for someone outside your field. What would you emphasize or leave out?
structure: Lead with the key point.
Explain one useful example in familiar language.
Check whether the listener needs more detail.
look_for: A clear message and accessible language.
mistakes: Replacing explanation with unexplained jargon.

questions.title: Reflect on a revision
questions.prompt: Show a change you made after feedback or testing. Why did you revise it, and what would you do next?
structure: Explain the original choice and feedback.
Describe the revision and what you checked.
Name a realistic next improvement.
mistakes: Presenting a planned change as already completed.

guides.title: Other interview formats
guides.intro: Use this guide when your preparation does not fit the named formats. Describe the actual format, field, audience and instructions before choosing how to practice.

blocks.title: Define what you are preparing for
blocks.text: Identify whether you need a panel discussion, an unfamiliar task, a role-specific conversation or another format. Add the instructions in setup; do not assume a company name tells us the format.

blocks.title: Match the answer to the task
blocks.text: A past-experience question needs a real example. A hypothetical problem needs assumptions and reasoning. A presentation needs an audience and purpose. Ask for clarification when the task is ambiguous.

blocks.title: Choose your next step
blocks.text: Use an adaptable prompt below, start without a question, or enter a question you already have. Follow-up discussion and personalized AI questions remain available inside the session.

questions.title: Clarify an unfamiliar brief
questions.prompt: Imagine an interviewer gives you an unfamiliar task with little detail. How would you clarify the objective, expected output and constraints before starting?
structure: Restate what is understood.
Ask the most consequential questions.
State a reasonable first step and remaining assumptions.
mistakes: Pretending the instructions are clear when they are not.

questions.title: Address different perspectives
questions.prompt: How would you explain one piece of your real work to a panel whose members have different levels of subject knowledge?
structure: Find a shared purpose.
Give a concise explanation and concrete example.
Invite and address questions at the right level.
mistakes: Assuming all panel members need the same technical detail.

questions.title: Respond when you do not know
questions.prompt: If an interviewer asks about an unfamiliar concept, how would you respond honestly while showing a useful way to reason or learn?
structure: State what you know and what you do not.
Ask a clarifying question or reason from a known principle.
Explain how you would verify your answer.
look_for: Honesty and a practical verification path.
mistakes: Making up a definition or claiming expertise.

questions.title: Ask a useful closing question
questions.prompt: Choose two questions you would ask an interviewer to understand the work, expectations or team. Explain why each matters to you.
structure: Identify information you still need.
Ask focused questions that cannot be answered by a quick page scan.
Connect the answer to an informed decision.
look_for: Curiosity tied to the actual work.
mistakes: Inventing facts about the employer.
